The ATP, with Puppo’s research help, has altered the record book before. Three clay-court titles were added to Vilas’s career total this year, bringing it to 49, after it was discovered that the tournaments’ surfaces had been incorrectly recorded.
While expressing appreciation for the extensive research effort, Kermode said that changing the rankings retroactively would create too many side effects. He cited the fact that if the rankings had been different, then tournament seedings would have been different, meaning players would have faced different opponents.
“It would be like in 50 years’ time, we work out that someone would have been ranked top five in this era if we went back and did it on an hourly basis,” Kermode said.
Kermode also said the basis for the WTA’s decision on Goolagong was different because it involved correcting a ranking that had been released.
“There were just some records missing, which is a bit different to us,” Kermode said. “We’ve got loads of records missing, but even so, the rankings were done 13 times that year. We’re not talking about missing weeks. It’s just that the rankings were simply not published on a weekly basis at that time.”
Until the ATP rankings began, the world rankings were more subjective, produced by some national federations, some leading media outlets and by individual journalists, including Lance Tingay in Britain and Bud Collins in the United States.
These were generally year-end rankings. The problem was that without a definitive system, it could be difficult for a talented and obscure player to secure a spot in tournaments, where entry lists were often determined by a star system or by tournament directors’ personal allegiances.
According to officials who worked on the ATP rankings in the early years, the primary reason for creating the rankings was not to designate a No. 1 but to create a reliable entry system.
Even after 1973, the other year-end rankings held sway with the public, and even the players, when it came to assessing the best of the best.
“Honestly, in the 1970s, no one, including the ATP, considered the No. 1 player on the ATP rankings the No. 1 player in the world,” said Dennis Spencer, who joined the ATP as a public relations employee in 1975 and later had primary responsibility for publishing the rankings.
It was a system based on an average of a player’s results, and it often rewarded top players who played fewer tournaments. Vilas was a workhorse, which is how he managed not to reach
No. 1 in the ATP rankings in 1977, when he won the French Open, the
United States Open
and 14 other tournaments.
Calculating and publishing the rankings was quite a challenge in the early years — a big reason the rankings were not released more often.
“When the ATP was in L.A. in 1975, Bobby Kramer used to take them down to TRW, the aerospace company, to their mainframe to run them down there,” Spencer said. “So that was another bit of a variable.”
The first No. 1 was Ilie Nastase, on Aug. 23 1973, followed on June 3, 1974, by John Newcombe before Connors took over for 160 weeks on July 29, 1974.

Spencer said generating interest in the early ATP rankings was an uphill slog, which is hard to believe from a modern perspective as changes at the top generate worldwide headlines.
Richard Evans, a member of the ATP ranking committee in 1975, said he could not recall any complaint about Vilas’s ranking at the time.
Though Vilas was No. 1 according to some experts and year-end ranking lists in 1977, Borg finished on top in the ATP rankings.
“Look, if somebody deserved to be No. 1, obviously you would like them to be able to have the accolades,” said Harold Solomon, one of Vilas’s former rivals and later a president of the ATP. “But I think it’s unfair to some degree to go back and reopen that conversation unless you reopen everything from everybody.”
Puppo, after seven years of analysis, feels differently.
“Should you not recognize a No. 1 because they happened not to publish a ranking because of the decision of some ATP employee or executive?” he said. “Is this more important than what a player did on the court?”
Puppo has not ruled out legal action, which he views as a last resort. Vilas, who has been following the situation closely, declined an interview request through an intermediary. Puppo said that he spoke with Vilas on Saturday and that Vilas was deeply disappointed.
“He is very hurt by all this,” Puppo said.
Kermode is sympathetic but firm.
“We just can’t adopt this version of rankings as official history; otherwise you would have everyone coming in and saying the same thing,” he said. “Where do you stop?”

Sony Pictures Entertainment on Sunday said that it had closed a deal to bring “
Beautiful: The Carole King Musical
” to the big screen.
Sony’s decision to bring “Beautiful” to multiplexes is not entirely unexpected. The studio’s corporate sibling, Sony/ATV owns most of the music rights, and “Beautiful” has been a breakout success on Broadway. Featured songs include “The Locomotion,” “(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman” and “So Far Away.”
But musicals — even ones based on stage smash hits — are among Hollywood’s riskiest propositions. Disney’s “
Into the Woods
” succeeded in finding an audience last year, but recent adaptations of “Jersey Boys” and “Rock of Ages” have fallen flat. Sony was pleased with the performance of “
Annie
,” released last Christmas, but box-office analysts were unimpressed.
The film version of “Beautiful” will be produced by Tom Hanks; Gary Goetzman, a producer whose movie credits include “Mamma Mia!” in 2008; and Paul Blake, the lead producer of “Beautiful” on Broadway. Douglas McGrath, who wrote the book for the stage production, will work on the screenplay.
No casting decisions were announced. “Beautiful” is now in its second year on Broadway. A London production opened last month, and a North American touring production is slated to begin in the fall.
“Audiences both on Broadway and in the West End have responded to ‘Beautiful’ not only to relive Carole King’s timeless classics, but to experience the ways they illustrate her triumphant and joyful life story,” Michael De Luca, a senior Sony movie executive, said in a statement.
